title: Activate a New Plugin on Selected Multisite Sites Only
description: A test plugin ZIP is already in plugins/. List every site on the network, activate the plugin only on two pilot URLs, and prove the main site stayed inactive — without using --network.
instructions: Type each command in the terminal below. The terminal validates your input at every step. Hints describe the action — not the exact command. Assume you are already in the WordPress root (document root).

steps.hint: List every site on this multisite network with blog_id and URL
steps.feedback_wrong: Start by listing sites — you need real URLs before you can choose a whitelist.
steps.feedback_correct: Three sites. Pilot plan: activate on /a/ and /b/ only. Leave the main site (blog_id 1) alone.

steps.hint: Confirm the plugin is installed but not active yet (by slug)
steps.feedback_wrong: Check the plugin by slug before activating — status should still be inactive on this bootstrap.
steps.feedback_correct: Files are there; status is inactive. Do not use --network — that would turn it on for every site.

steps.hint: Activate the plugin on the first pilot site only (/a/)
steps.output:
Plugin 'my-plugin' activated.
Success: Activated 1 of 1 plugins.
steps.feedback_wrong: Activate with --url pointing at the first pilot path (/a/), not --network.
steps.feedback_correct: First pilot is live. One more pilot URL to go — still no --network.

steps.hint: Activate the plugin on the second pilot site only (/b/)
steps.output:
Plugin 'my-plugin' activated.
Success: Activated 1 of 1 plugins.
steps.feedback_wrong: Same pattern as the previous step — --url for /b/ only.
steps.feedback_correct: Both pilots are active. Now prove the main site is still inactive.

steps.hint: Read plugin status on the network main site (no /a/ or /b/ path)
steps.feedback_wrong: Query status with --url set to the main site root — the one you deliberately left out of the whitelist.
steps.feedback_correct: Main site is still inactive — per-site pilot worked. Optionally check /a/ and /b/ next; both should report active.

steps.hint: Confirm status on one pilot site returns active
steps.feedback_wrong: Check --field=status with --url set to either pilot (/a/ or /b/).
steps.feedback_correct: Whitelist holds: pilots active, main site inactive. Never reach for --network on a staged plugin test.

content.goal: On a WordPress Multisite network, list every site, activate a newly delivered plugin only on whitelisted pilot URLs with --url, and verify the remaining sites stayed inactive — without network-wide activation.

steps.title: 1. List sites before you touch activation
paragraphs: Multisite keeps one shared plugins/ folder. Activation can still be per site. You cannot build a whitelist without the live URL list.
Always run WP-CLI from the WordPress document root. Relative includes such as wp-salt.php fail if you launch wp from plugins/ or another subdirectory — a frequent trap on managed cloud panels.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the plugin is present and inactive
paragraphs: After unzip into wp-content/plugins/, WordPress should see the slug as inactive (or not network-active).
This challenge assumes the ZIP is already extracted. On a real host you unzip, then cd back to the WordPress root before any wp command.

steps.title: 3–4. Activate only the pilot URLs
paragraphs: Use wp plugin activate {slug} --url=… for each allowed site. Do not pass --network for a staged or regional pilot.
Anything not in the whitelist simply never gets an activate call — that is your denylist.

steps.title: 5–6. Verify status across sites
paragraphs: Read status with --url for the main site and at least one pilot. Expect inactive on the root, active on pilots.
On a real SSH session you can loop wp site list --field=url and print status for every URL in one pass.

non_enterprise: Managed cloud / agency hosts (panel + SSH into an app folder): expect paths like ~/applications/{app_id}/public_html, relative salt files, and quiet GoPricing/PHP notices in CLI noise.
Master SSH often lands outside the WordPress root — always cd into the document root before wp.
Staging and production may be separate apps on the same server; never assume one APP id.
Per-site activate is the default safe story for pilots: fewer approval layers, but also fewer guardrails — your whitelist is the process.
enterprise: Enterprise WordPress platforms usually add change windows, ticket IDs, and audited deploys. Document the whitelist (blog_id + URL) in the ticket before you run activate.
Prefer artifact deploy (CI → release ZIP) over ad-hoc scp when policy requires it; still activate with --url unless the change is approved network-wide.
--network without sign-off is a governance failure, not just a technical one — roll back with deactivate --network then re-apply per-site.
Expect object-cache / page-cache flushes and read-only filesystem quirks; verify status via WP-CLI and an admin smoke test on each pilot hostname.

troubleshooting: Failed opening required 'wp-salt.php' — WP-CLI was started outside the WordPress root (common after cd …/plugins on managed cloud). Run cd back to the document root and retry.
Using --network — turns the plugin on for every site. Deactivate network-wide, then activate per --url for the whitelist only.
Activating without --url on Multisite — often hits the main site only, which is not the same as a deliberate pilot list.
Sub-site admin shows the plugin as missing or inactive — it was never activated for that site's URL.
wp site list empty or wrong — wrong document root / app path on a multi-app managed host.

faq.question: When should I use --network instead of --url?
faq.answer: Use --network only when every site in the network must load the plugin immediately (and, on enterprise stacks, when that is ticket-approved). For pilots, regional rollouts, or staging tests, activate with --url per site.

faq.question: Does installing the ZIP activate the plugin?
faq.answer: No. Unzip only places files under wp-content/plugins/. Activation is a separate Multisite decision — network-wide or per site.

faq.question: Why does WP-CLI die with wp-salt.php on some hosts?
faq.answer: Some managed cloud stacks load salts via a relative require. If your shell cwd is not the WordPress root, that relative path fails. Change directory to the document root before running wp. Enterprise platforms may hide this behind wrappers — still treat wrong cwd as the first checklist item.

faq.question: How do I know who is allowed and who is not?
faq.answer: Build an explicit whitelist from wp site list. Activate only those URLs. Every other site stays inactive until you deliberately add it — no separate denylist command is required.

faq.question: Is a typical managed cloud host “enterprise”?
faq.answer: No. Managed cloud panels aimed at agencies and mid-market teams are not the same as enterprise WordPress platforms with contractual change control. The WP-CLI commands are identical; the process around them is not — cover both accents in runbooks.

seo.title: Multisite Per-Site Plugin Activation with WP-CLI — Practice Case
seo.description: Practice listing Multisite URLs and activating a plugin only on whitelisted sites with --url — never --network. Covers managed cloud cwd traps and enterprise change-control notes. Interactive WP-CLI terminal.

perfect: You listed sites first and activated only the pilot URLs with --url.
You verified the main site stayed inactive instead of trusting a single Success line.
optimize: On managed cloud hosts, unzip then immediately cd back to the WordPress root before any wp command.
On enterprise hosts, paste the whitelist into the change ticket before you activate — and script a status loop over every URL.
